We asked the No on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
Because of the requirements it imposes on new special taxes, voting “yes” could also mean that Proposition 40 (the “billionaire tax”), even if it gets enough votes, is stopped from becoming law if the courts determine that it conflicts with Prop. 41.
Voting “no” would mean that the state auditor’s role in reviewing government programs stays the same, as would spending limit requirements.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Prohibit Excluding New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Require Special Tax Audits Initiative, favor the increased transparency, oversight and analysis regarding special taxes. More information for the voters.
Generally, opponents don’t like the extra restrictions on how voter-approved tax money is raised and spent and how the programs meant to be funded could be weakened or stalled. They also suggest that Props. 41 and 42 were heavily supported by billionaires in order to defeat Prop. 40.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/).
What’s the strongest argument against Prop. 41?
Prop. 41 was put on the ballot for one reason — because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share in taxes. This initiative was created to trick voters into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce.
One of Prop. 41’s main funders is Google founder Sergey Brin, whose wealth has doubled to nearly $300 billion. Now he’s spent tens of millions of dollars to fund this sham measure that attempts to cancel out the billionaire tax.
But Prop. 41 isn’t just a scheme, it’s an expensive one. It would require pre-election and ongoing audits of state programs that are funded by new special taxes, costing the state time and money. California already has extensive audit requirements and an independent state auditor who regularly issues reports on state operations.
This initiative isn’t about helping Californians — it’s about billionaires avoiding a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
Don’t voters deserve an unbiased look at how their money will be spent before they vote on a new tax?
California already has an independent state auditor and extensive audit requirements. Prop. 41 goes beyond providing voters with information. It requires a pre-election audit of programs that would receive special-tax revenue, which isn’t only not possible, it interferes with the existing authority of the state auditor.
In addition, any change in audit rules should not undermine the only viable response to $100 billion in federal health care cuts under H.R. 1. Prop. 40 would use funds generated by the billionaire tax to keep hospitals and ERs open, as well as fund health care services that Californians count on like Medicaid and marketplace coverage under the Affordable Care Act. These are all programs that California taxpayers currently fund, and that the Trump administration cut by $100 billion dollars over the next five years. Prop. 40 would backfill those cuts.
What is wrong with forcing government programs to find 10% in cost savings to protect taxpayer dollars?
There’s nothing wrong with finding genuine savings and improving services that California taxpayers support and rely upon. The problem with Prop. 41 is that that is the role of the state auditor, not Sergey Brin.
Prop. 41 doesn’t simply require programs to identify waste. Its audit framework specifically requires recommendations for achieving at least 10% annual budgetary savings and comparisons with analogous private-sector programs.
Those are very different things.
A program may be expensive because the service itself is expensive — not because 10% of its funding is wasted. That’s particularly important for health care, where costs can reflect the escalating costs of prescription drugs, a rapidly aging population, provider shortages and changing federal requirements.
A good government should identify waste, fraud and inefficiency. But that requires evidence, not an arbitrary savings target imposed across fundamentally different programs.
You argue this is a strategy by billionaires to avoid paying taxes. Can you explain exactly how Prop. 41 would block the Prop. 40 wealth tax?
Yes, it hinges on Prop. 41’s Gann Limit provision.
Prop. 41 prohibits collecting state taxes enacted or taking effect after January 1, 2026 if they rely on an exemption or exclusion from the state’s Gann spending limit, which Prop. 40 does.
That’s important because Prop. 40 is a special tax initiative with revenues dedicated to health care services. Without the ability to structure the tax and its spending outside the Gann Limit, the estimated revenue of $100 billion cannot be spent as voters intended.
Prop. 41 creates a new constitutional restriction that directly conflicts with the fiscal structure Prop. 40 requires. Exceptions to the Gann limit are common, and the Gann limit itself, which ties the government to what it spent and prioritized in 1979, is just poor public policy.
If Prop. 41 fails, how else do you suggest California ensure that special tax revenues are being spent efficiently?
California already has mechanisms to do that. The state has extensive audit requirements and an independent state auditor that regularly examines state operations and issues public reports. We should use and strengthen those mechanisms where necessary. The better approach is targeted oversight: audit programs, evaluate outcomes, identify waste or fraud, publish the findings and hold policymakers accountable.
Why should people opposed to Prop. 40 also vote against Prop. 41?
Because Prop. 41 is not limited to Prop. 40. Prop. 41 is likely to endanger other revenue measures, including education funding, taxes connected to Medi-Cal and other health care financing mechanisms.
For instance, Prop. 41 could subject Prop. 3 — the education-funding measure — to its new audit rules. If Prop. 41 receives more votes, it could thereby put Prop. 3’s tax extension at risk of being struck down because of the conflicting language. It could also similarly threaten Medi-Cal taxes and fees that bring the state billions of dollars in federal matching funds.
So someone can oppose Prop. 40 on its merits and still conclude that Prop. 41 goes too far.

CalCPA Takes Positions on November Tax Measures
CalCPA opposes the billionaire wealth tax due to significant tax administration concerns; supports independent audits of taxpayer-funded programs; and supports constitutional protections against retroactive taxation.
By CalCPA Staff
Aug. 24, 2026
AUG. 25, 2026 | SACRAMENTO, CA —CalCPA (https://www.calcpa.org/), the statewide association representing California's CPA profession, announced its positions on three measures on the Nov. 3 statewide ballot (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/qualified-ballot-measures). CalCPA opposes Proposition 40 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40.pdf), the “2026 Billionaire Tax Act,” and supports Proposition 41 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop41.pdf), the “Improving Transparency, Effectiveness, and Efficiency in California Government Act of 2026,” and supports Proposition 42 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42.pdf), the “Retirement & Personal Savings Protection Act of 2026.” CalCPA is also a signer of the official ballot argument in support of Proposition 41.
CalCPA’s positions are grounded in the profession’s expertise in tax, auditing and financial accountability, along with its longstanding commitment to the public interest. Because CPAs help taxpayers navigate California’s tax laws and assess whether programs and controls are effective, CalCPA evaluated each measure for fair, consistent and predictable implementation, as well as its potential effects on accountability and public confidence.
“Our positions reflect the accounting profession’s longstanding work to advance sound public policy,” said Denise LeDuc Froemming, CPA, President and CEO of CalCPA. “Every day, CPAs help California taxpayers, businesses and nonprofit organizations navigate complex tax laws and provide independent assurance that builds public trust. We evaluated each measure through that practical lens because Californians deserve tax policies that are clear, workable and accountable.”
Oppose Proposition 40—The 2026 Billionaire Tax Act
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5 percent tax on individuals and trusts with more than $1 billion in covered assets, payable over five years. CalCPA opposes the measure because it creates a fundamentally new and difficult-to-administer tax framework that raises significant administrative feasibility concerns. The proposal relies on valuing complex and often illiquid assets, increasing the likelihood of valuation disputes, litigation and uncertainty for taxpayers, tax practitioners and tax agencies. In addition, its retroactive tax provisions undermine taxpayer certainty by changing the rules after the fact. The Legislative Analyst's Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis) analysis of Proposition 40 notes many of these practical implementation concerns and long-term risks to income tax revenues from taxpayer behaviors in response to the measure.
Support Proposition 41—Improving Transparency, Effectiveness and Efficiency in California Government Act
Proposition 41 requires the independent California State Auditor (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/) to conduct pre-election and ongoing performance and financial audits of programs funded by new statewide special taxes, with audit results made available to voters. The measure also requires new state taxes to remain subject to California's existing voter-approved state spending limit.
CalCPA supports Proposition 41 because independent audits provide voters with objective, credible information to inform decisions about public spending. Transparency, sound data and independent review are essential to effective governance and reflect principles central to the CPA profession.
CPAs provide businesses, nonprofits, governments and the public with reliable information that supports sound decision-making. Proposition 41 applies these principles, giving Californians useful information to evaluate public programs, inform resource allocation and promote responsible fiscal management. CalCPA is proud to sign the official ballot argument in support of Proposition 41.
Support Proposition 42—Retirement & Personal Savings Protection Act
Prop 42 would amend the California Constitution to prohibit new state taxes on personal property, including retirement accounts, financial assets, business interests and intellectual property, while also limiting certain retroactive state taxes.
CalCPA supports the measure because stable, prospective tax policy promotes taxpayer certainty and reinforces confidence that the rules will not change after the fact. Clear and predictable tax laws make California's tax system easier to administer, easier for taxpayers to comply with and more consistent with sound principles of tax administration.

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 5:03 PM PST | UPDATED: November 3, 2026 at 4:35 AM PST
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 41, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026), would require an audit on new or increased special taxes before they appear on the ballot and ongoing audits of programs that receive funding from special taxes. Special taxes may also be subjected to spending limits.
Voting “yes” would mean that the state auditor reviews programs funded by special taxes before they’re on the ballot and on an ongoing basis while opening the possibility that spending limits are attached to the special taxes.

We asked the No on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
Because of the requirements it imposes on new special taxes, voting “yes” could also mean that Proposition 40 (the “billionaire tax”), even if it gets enough votes, is stopped from becoming law if the courts determine that it conflicts with Prop. 41.
Voting “no” would mean that the state auditor’s role in reviewing government programs stays the same, as would spending limit requirements.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Prohibit Excluding New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Require Special Tax Audits Initiative, favor the increased transparency, oversight and analysis regarding special taxes. More information for the voters.
Generally, opponents don’t like the extra restrictions on how voter-approved tax money is raised and spent and how the programs meant to be funded could be weakened or stalled. They also suggest that Props. 41 and 42 were heavily supported by billionaires in order to defeat Prop. 40.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem is Prop. 41 solving?
State spending is up 79% since 2019. Every year, billions of taxpayer dollars flow into state programs, like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it. Californians deserve better education, health care, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned tax money we pay to the state.
While this is a city wide example, it’s exactly the kind of reason why we need audits and transparent accountability before it’s too late to put programs back on track: Audit: San Jose failed to adequately track $300 million in homelessness spending (https://www.mercurynews.com/2024/04/13/audit-san-jose-failed-to-adequately-track-300-million-in-homelessness-spending/).
Why is this the best solution to the problem?
Prop. 41 requires the independent state auditor to conduct financial and performance audits of the programs to be funded by new special tax measures, with the results posted publicly in the state Voter Information Guide.
This ensures voters have detailed information about the programs they’re being asked to raise taxes to fund.
If taxes are approved, Prop. 41 also requires ongoing public audits of the programs funded by those taxes to evaluate spending, identify waste, fraud or abuse, assess whether they are meeting their intended goals and recommend improvements.
It also requires that all new taxes comply with the state’s voter-approved spending limit — so that excess tax revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
Why is it necessary to audit a tax proposal before it even officially qualifies for the ballot?
Providing pre-ballot information about proposed initiatives is very typical. The Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) and the attorney general are required by state law to provide pre-ballot information on every measure that is filed.
Prop. 41 is actually much narrower — the auditor only commences with an audit once a measure collects 25% of the signatures needed to qualify for the ballot; and it only applies to initiatives that increase taxes.
Prop. 41 requires the independent state auditor to conduct pre-election financial and performance audits of the programs to be funded by proposed new state special taxes. The state auditor’s findings must be shared widely with the public, including in the state’s official Voter Information Guide.
This pre-election audit will give voters clear, unbiased information on the programs a proposed tax would support. These audits are more extensive than any existing information provided to voters. This fills in a critical gap in the information provided to voters. The current initiative analyses from the LAO are required by law to provide only a description of the measure. Alternatively, under Prop. 41 the auditor will also provide voters a performance evaluation of programs funded by new taxes.
If a proposed tax fails to make the ballot, the state’s general fund still has to pay for the audit. Why should taxpayers foot the bill for failed political ideas?
The value to voters in seeing this detailed information about programs before they’re asked to vote far outweighs the marginal cost of conducting the audit and printing it in the Voter Guide.
Again, this is very typical under the status quo. The LAO and the attorney general already have to provide a description and a title and summary for each and every initiative measure — including those that fail — and the General Fund pays for those costs. It is also important to recognize that the extra costs imposed on the General Fund by Prop. 41 are exceedingly small. The LAO found that Prop. 41 would impose only minimal costs upon the General Fund. Further, providing more impartial, expert information to voters when decided to approve higher taxes is money well spent.
This also fails to take into account Prop. 41’s upside. As the LAO noted in the Voter Guide, Prop. 41 would result in taxpayer savings or improved services by implementing the auditor’s recommendations.
Prop. 41 contains conflict provisions stating that if it receives more “yes” votes than a competing tax measure like Prop. 40 (the billionaire wealth tax), then Prop. 40 is nullified entirely. How do proponents respond to claims that Prop. 41 is merely a “poison pill” designed to defeat the wealth tax rather than a stand-alone oversight tool?
California has faced issues with ineffective and inefficient state spending for years: homelessness, state technology programs, EDD are just a few recent examples. Prop. 40 is just the latest proposal that would fuel ineffective spending.
Prop. 40 seeks to raise tens of billions of dollars in new tax revenue, but contains zero transparency, accountability or safeguards to ensure the money is spent as intended. For instance, Prop. 40 contains no safeguards to ensure that billions of dollars don’t flow to health insurance company profits and CEOs under the guise of “saving health care.”
Prop. 40 also exempts itself from the state spending limit, so that the billions in excess tax revenues generated by the measure that would normally flow to taxpayers, schools and the state rainy day fund instead go to the Legislature with no safeguards or accountability. Prop. 41 makes sure measures like Prop. 40 can’t rip off taxpayers and schools by exempting themselves from the state spending limit.

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 41, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026), would require an audit on new or increased special taxes before they appear on the ballot and ongoing audits of programs that receive funding from special taxes. Special taxes may also be subjected to spending limits.
Voting “yes” would mean that the state auditor reviews programs funded by special taxes before they’re on the ballot and on an ongoing basis while opening the possibility that spending limits are attached to the special taxes.

We asked the No on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
Because of the requirements it imposes on new special taxes, voting “yes” could also mean that Proposition 40 (the “billionaire tax”), even if it gets enough votes, is stopped from becoming law if the courts determine that it conflicts with Prop. 41.
Voting “no” would mean that the state auditor’s role in reviewing government programs stays the same, as would spending limit requirements.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Prohibit Excluding New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Require Special Tax Audits Initiative, favor the increased transparency, oversight and analysis regarding special taxes. More information for the voters.
Generally, opponents don’t like the extra restrictions on how voter-approved tax money is raised and spent and how the programs meant to be funded could be weakened or stalled. They also suggest that Props. 41 and 42 were heavily supported by billionaires in order to defeat Prop. 40.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/).
What’s the strongest argument against Prop. 41?
Prop. 41 was put on the ballot for one reason — because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share in taxes. This initiative was created to trick voters into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce.
One of Prop. 41’s main funders is Google founder Sergey Brin, whose wealth has doubled to nearly $300 billion. Now he’s spent tens of millions of dollars to fund this sham measure that attempts to cancel out the billionaire tax.
But Prop. 41 isn’t just a scheme, it’s an expensive one. It would require pre-election and ongoing audits of state programs that are funded by new special taxes, costing the state time and money. California already has extensive audit requirements and an independent state auditor who regularly issues reports on state operations.
This initiative isn’t about helping Californians — it’s about billionaires avoiding a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
Don’t voters deserve an unbiased look at how their money will be spent before they vote on a new tax?
California already has an independent state auditor and extensive audit requirements. Prop. 41 goes beyond providing voters with information. It requires a pre-election audit of programs that would receive special-tax revenue, which isn’t only not possible, it interferes with the existing authority of the state auditor.
In addition, any change in audit rules should not undermine the only viable response to $100 billion in federal health care cuts under H.R. 1. Prop. 40 would use funds generated by the billionaire tax to keep hospitals and ERs open, as well as fund health care services that Californians count on like Medicaid and marketplace coverage under the Affordable Care Act. These are all programs that California taxpayers currently fund, and that the Trump administration cut by $100 billion dollars over the next five years. Prop. 40 would backfill those cuts.
What is wrong with forcing government programs to find 10% in cost savings to protect taxpayer dollars?
There’s nothing wrong with finding genuine savings and improving services that California taxpayers support and rely upon. The problem with Prop. 41 is that that is the role of the state auditor, not Sergey Brin.
Prop. 41 doesn’t simply require programs to identify waste. Its audit framework specifically requires recommendations for achieving at least 10% annual budgetary savings and comparisons with analogous private-sector programs.
Those are very different things.
A program may be expensive because the service itself is expensive — not because 10% of its funding is wasted. That’s particularly important for health care, where costs can reflect the escalating costs of prescription drugs, a rapidly aging population, provider shortages and changing federal requirements.
A good government should identify waste, fraud and inefficiency. But that requires evidence, not an arbitrary savings target imposed across fundamentally different programs.
You argue this is a strategy by billionaires to avoid paying taxes. Can you explain exactly how Prop. 41 would block the Prop. 40 wealth tax?
Yes, it hinges on Prop. 41’s Gann Limit provision.
Prop. 41 prohibits collecting state taxes enacted or taking effect after January 1, 2026 if they rely on an exemption or exclusion from the state’s Gann spending limit, which Prop. 40 does.
That’s important because Prop. 40 is a special tax initiative with revenues dedicated to health care services. Without the ability to structure the tax and its spending outside the Gann Limit, the estimated revenue of $100 billion cannot be spent as voters intended.
Prop. 41 creates a new constitutional restriction that directly conflicts with the fiscal structure Prop. 40 requires. Exceptions to the Gann limit are common, and the Gann limit itself, which ties the government to what it spent and prioritized in 1979, is just poor public policy.
If Prop. 41 fails, how else do you suggest California ensure that special tax revenues are being spent efficiently?
California already has mechanisms to do that. The state has extensive audit requirements and an independent state auditor that regularly examines state operations and issues public reports. We should use and strengthen those mechanisms where necessary. The better approach is targeted oversight: audit programs, evaluate outcomes, identify waste or fraud, publish the findings and hold policymakers accountable.
Why should people opposed to Prop. 40 also vote against Prop. 41?
Because Prop. 41 is not limited to Prop. 40. Prop. 41 is likely to endanger other revenue measures, including education funding, taxes connected to Medi-Cal and other health care financing mechanisms.
For instance, Prop. 41 could subject Prop. 3 — the education-funding measure — to its new audit rules. If Prop. 41 receives more votes, it could thereby put Prop. 3’s tax extension at risk of being struck down because of the conflicting language. It could also similarly threaten Medi-Cal taxes and fees that bring the state billions of dollars in federal matching funds.
So someone can oppose Prop. 40 on its merits and still conclude that Prop. 41 goes too far.

so that the billions in excess tax revenues generated by the measure that would normally flow to taxpayers, schools and the state rainy day fund instead go to the Legislature with no safeguards or accountability. Prop. 41 makes sure measures like Prop. 40 can’t rip off taxpayers and schools by exempting themselves from the state spending limit.
The measure requires the state auditor to find a way to cut an audited program’s costs by 10%. Why mandate a flat 10% cut for every program, regardless of how it operates?
Prop. 41 does not in any way mandate a 10% cut for every program. What Prop. 41 actually says is that the auditor’s report should contain recommendations on how the program could achieve a budgetary savings of 10%. There is no mandate — this is simply one of several factors (at least 10) that the auditor must address when evaluating new spending. The point is to give voters context: For some programs a 10% budget savings may be a good idea and for others it won’t. But right now voters are totally in the dark. Exploring ways to stretch taxpayer dollars farther is always a good idea. But there is no mandate.
The sponsor of Prop. 41 is primarily backed by one billionaire. What makes Prop. 41’s billionaire backer a policy expert capable of devising smart laws for 40 million people?
Prop. 41 is supported by Build Better California, but also has a broad and diverse coalition of organizations and advocacy groups working toward a more transparent California, including small businesses, taxpayers, good government advocates, elected officials, accountants and auditing experts. Specifically, the ballot arguments in support of Prop. 41 were signed by the California Society of Certified Public Accountants, the California Taxpayers Association, a former California State Auditor, the Asian Pacific Islander Chamber of Commerce and former State Controller Steve Westly.
Why should someone in favor of Prop. 40 vote for Prop. 41?
As stated above, state spending is up and billions of dollars are wasted each year in programs that, while well intended, have failed to deliver on the promises made. Prop. 41, by way of the independent State Auditor, will ensure Californians get more accountability, transparency and trackable progress of programs funded by our taxes, so that we stop funding failure and start funding successful outcomes. If both Prop. 40 and Prop. 41 pass and 40 gets more votes, Prop. 41’s provisions will still go into effect to the benefit of voters and taxpayers.
What is the biggest logical error opponents of Prop. 41 make?
Prop. 41’s opponents are all proponents of more taxes and more spending regardless of the accountability, oversight, transparency or trackable metrics needed to help improve the results we get for our tax dollars.
The California State Auditor’s Office is absolutely first-rate and does a fantastic job providing unbiased, nonpartisan, objective information. Getting this type of information to voters, both as part of the Voter Guide and on an ongoing basis (for taxes that are approved), is something that we should have done long ago.
What did we miss? What else should we know?
Voters support the idea of more transparency and accountability. Recent polling shows that 58% support the concept of Prop. 41:
“Q: this measure would require the independent State Auditor to conduct public performance and financial audits of the programs to be funded by proposed new taxes. Knowing this, do you support or oppose this proposal?”

so that the billions in excess tax revenues generated by the measure that would normally flow to taxpayers, schools and the state rainy day fund instead go to the Legislature with no safeguards or accountability. Prop. 41 makes sure measures like Prop. 40 can’t rip off taxpayers and schools by exempting themselves from the state spending limit.
The measure requires the state auditor to find a way to cut an audited program’s costs by 10%. Why mandate a flat 10% cut for every program, regardless of how it operates?
Prop. 41 does not in any way mandate a 10% cut for every program. What Prop. 41 actually says is that the auditor’s report should contain recommendations on how the program could achieve a budgetary savings of 10%. There is no mandate — this is simply one of several factors (at least 10) that the auditor must address when evaluating new spending. The point is to give voters context: For some programs a 10% budget savings may be a good idea and for others it won’t. But right now voters are totally in the dark. Exploring ways to stretch taxpayer dollars farther is always a good idea. But there is no mandate.
The sponsor of Prop. 41 is primarily backed by one billionaire. What makes Prop. 41’s billionaire backer a policy expert capable of devising smart laws for 40 million people?
Prop. 41 is supported by Build Better California, but also has a broad and diverse coalition of organizations and advocacy groups working toward a more transparent California, including small businesses, taxpayers, good government advocates, elected officials, accountants and auditing experts. Specifically, the ballot arguments in support of Prop. 41 were signed by the California Society of Certified Public Accountants, the California Taxpayers Association, a former California State Auditor, the Asian Pacific Islander Chamber of Commerce and former State Controller Steve Westly.
Why should someone in favor of Prop. 40 vote for Prop. 41?
As stated above, state spending is up and billions of dollars are wasted each year in programs that, while well intended, have failed to deliver on the promises made. Prop. 41, by way of the independent State Auditor, will ensure Californians get more accountability, transparency and trackable progress of programs funded by our taxes, so that we stop funding failure and start funding successful outcomes. If both Prop. 40 and Prop. 41 pass and 40 gets more votes, Prop. 41’s provisions will still go into effect to the benefit of voters and taxpayers.
What is the biggest logical error opponents of Prop. 41 make?
Prop. 41’s opponents are all proponents of more taxes and more spending regardless of the accountability, oversight, transparency or trackable metrics needed to help improve the results we get for our tax dollars.
The California State Auditor’s Office is absolutely first-rate and does a fantastic job providing unbiased, nonpartisan, objective information. Getting this type of information to voters, both as part of the Voter Guide and on an ongoing basis (for taxes that are approved), is something that we should have done long ago.
What did we miss? What else should we know?
Voters support the idea of more transparency and accountability. Recent polling shows that 58% support the concept of Prop. 41:
“Q: this measure would require the independent State Auditor to conduct public performance and financial audits of the programs to be funded by proposed new taxes. Knowing this, do you support or oppose this proposal?”

so that the billions in excess tax revenues generated by the measure that would normally flow to taxpayers, schools and the state rainy day fund instead go to the Legislature with no safeguards or accountability. Prop. 41 makes sure measures like Prop. 40 can’t rip off taxpayers and schools by exempting themselves from the state spending limit.
The measure requires the state auditor to find a way to cut an audited program’s costs by 10%. Why mandate a flat 10% cut for every program, regardless of how it operates?
Prop. 41 does not in any way mandate a 10% cut for every program. What Prop. 41 actually says is that the auditor’s report should contain recommendations on how the program could achieve a budgetary savings of 10%. There is no mandate — this is simply one of several factors (at least 10) that the auditor must address when evaluating new spending. The point is to give voters context: For some programs a 10% budget savings may be a good idea and for others it won’t. But right now voters are totally in the dark. Exploring ways to stretch taxpayer dollars farther is always a good idea. But there is no mandate.
The sponsor of Prop. 41 is primarily backed by one billionaire. What makes Prop. 41’s billionaire backer a policy expert capable of devising smart laws for 40 million people?
Prop. 41 is supported by Build Better California, but also has a broad and diverse coalition of organizations and advocacy groups working toward a more transparent California, including small businesses, taxpayers, good government advocates, elected officials, accountants and auditing experts. Specifically, the ballot arguments in support of Prop. 41 were signed by the California Society of Certified Public Accountants, the California Taxpayers Association, a former California State Auditor, the Asian Pacific Islander Chamber of Commerce and former State Controller Steve Westly.
Why should someone in favor of Prop. 40 vote for Prop. 41?
As stated above, state spending is up and billions of dollars are wasted each year in programs that, while well intended, have failed to deliver on the promises made. Prop. 41, by way of the independent State Auditor, will ensure Californians get more accountability, transparency and trackable progress of programs funded by our taxes, so that we stop funding failure and start funding successful outcomes. If both Prop. 40 and Prop. 41 pass and 40 gets more votes, Prop. 41’s provisions will still go into effect to the benefit of voters and taxpayers.
What is the biggest logical error opponents of Prop. 41 make?
Prop. 41’s opponents are all proponents of more taxes and more spending regardless of the accountability, oversight, transparency or trackable metrics needed to help improve the results we get for our tax dollars.
The California State Auditor’s Office is absolutely first-rate and does a fantastic job providing unbiased, nonpartisan, objective information. Getting this type of information to voters, both as part of the Voter Guide and on an ongoing basis (for taxes that are approved), is something that we should have done long ago.
What did we miss? What else should we know?
Voters support the idea of more transparency and accountability. Recent polling shows that 58% support the concept of Prop. 41:
“Q: this measure would require the independent State Auditor to conduct public performance and financial audits of the programs to be funded by proposed new taxes. Knowing this, do you support or oppose this proposal?”

**Evaluating audit requirements**

I'm considering the argument around the 10% requirement in audits. It's described as a recommendation rather than a mandate, which is an important nuance. The campaign states there’s "no mandate," but it still requires auditor recommendations for savings. Critics might exaggerate the implications, saying it forces cuts, but in reality, it encourages suggestions. Even though they're just recommendations, they can influence the analysis. Also, auditing special-tax programs could provide independent evidence for voters but only for specific instances.**Analyzing special tax proposals**

I'm examining the focus on special taxes and how voters might want to understand their uses. The fiscal cap limit is a significant policy, and it’s not just about spending limits on special taxes; it applies the Gann cap to all revenue. Leaders can spend within limits but can add new taxes as long as they comply. This doesn't restrict new taxes but makes them subject to the Gann cap, which closes potential loopholes and allows excess funds for schools or rebates when the cap is exceeded.**Understanding state appropriation limits**

I'm looking at how the Constitution allows the Legislature to change the state appropriation limit through a law, specifically Section 4 of Article XIII B, which lets them raise this limit with a 2/3 vote for capital outlays. I need to clarify how Prop 41 defines exclusions—it mentions revenue outside the General Fund and certain appropriations that don't count against this limit. It also prohibits any state tax from increasing the spending cap through statute, creating a significant restriction on the Legislature's power.**Evaluating Prop41 language**

I need to check the text of Prop41, especially concerning the 10% process. The auditors are independent, and their reports don't have to mandate a 10% cut with evidence. They can suggest budgetary savings without judging if funding needs to be less. However, the phrase "at least 10 percent" could lead to issues if they can't find savings, potentially forcing arbitrary recommendations. Also, comparing private-sector programs might not offer a direct comparison to public programs like healthcare.**Assessing audit concerns**

I'm noticing some significant concerns about the audits. First, they need to identify how program costs stack up against similar programs in the non-government sector, but if none exist, that could be a problem. The pre-election audit summary will be included in a voter guide, which could be costly. It seems like the audit only happens once 25% of signatures are collected for a new tax measure, which complicates things. Perhaps this is more of an analysis rather than a performance audit since no funds have been allocated yet.**Analyzing campaign funding**

The user is asking about support for a proposition, and I’m looking at recent election-day articles from November 3. I need to check campaign funding, which shows $58.3 million backing from a billionaire PAC against union-backed opposition. It’s interesting to note the majority comes from Building a Better California, driven by tech billionaires like Sergey Brin. This indicates significant financial interest in the outcome. I can verify how the campaign's funds relate to previous propositions, especially opposition finance.**Exploring funding sources and implications**

I’m considering if the "top donor" group also funds support for Prop 42 and opposition to Prop 40, which has been confirmed. It looks like there isn't an external campaign pushing against this. The SEIU and similar organizations benefit from federal healthcare funding and support Prop 40, showing their significant interests in healthcare. Billionaires are also involved, contributing resources. There’s a historical aspect with Prop 10 concerning spending exemptions. Furthermore, Prop 41 may restrict future initiatives approved by the majority unless amendments are made.**Evaluating tax ballot measures**

The conflict provision in 41 introduces a higher voting requirement for future ballot measures that aim to exempt a tax from limitations. If a new tax measure receives more votes, it can override 41, but if it doesn't, it becomes void. This adds a significant hurdle for future proposed special taxes. Voters might pass a tax measure but not support the necessary spending limit exemption, potentially creating confusion around competing measures and their requirements for approval.**Analyzing future tax measures**

Not all future tax measures need to be co-balloted with Prop41. As long as Prop41 remains law and isn't repealed, passing a tax exempt from the cap is impossible. If a later measure amends Article XXIV and gets more yes votes than 41, it can override it. However, the same-ballot conflict clause only applies to measures on the same ballot as Prop41, meaning a later measure can potentially amend or repeal the earlier one in subsequent elections.**Understanding ballot measures**

The rules about co-balloting mean that a later election can amend previous measures without permanently needing to outvote Prop41 when another tax comes up. Still, the operational prohibition on tax exemptions from Article XXIV means that a new tax initiative must explicitly alter Prop41 to be valid. It’s not a steep challenge, as voters still have the power. The Prop41 conflict measure only applies if another measure is on the same ballot, while Prop40 has its own conflict section to prevent being defeated by 41 or 42.

The conflict provision in 41 introduces a higher voting requirement for future ballot measures that aim to exempt a tax from limitations. If a new tax measure receives more votes, it can override 41, but if it doesn't, it becomes void. This adds a significant hurdle for future proposed special taxes. Voters might pass a tax measure but not support the necessary spending limit exemption, potentially creating confusion around competing measures and their requirements for approval.**Analyzing future tax measures**

Not all future tax measures need to be co-balloted with Prop41. As long as Prop41 remains law and isn't repealed, passing a tax exempt from the cap is impossible. If a later measure amends Article XXIV and gets more yes votes than 41, it can override it. However, the same-ballot conflict clause only applies to measures on the same ballot as Prop41, meaning a later measure can potentially amend or repeal the earlier one in subsequent elections.**Understanding ballot measures**

The rules about co-balloting mean that a later election can amend previous measures without permanently needing to outvote Prop41 when another tax comes up. Still, the operational prohibition on tax exemptions from Article XXIV means that a new tax initiative must explicitly alter Prop41 to be valid. It’s not a steep challenge, as voters still have the power. About Us
About the California State Auditor
On this page:
How our work begins

2026 Peer Review results
Nonpartisan analyses for California’s policymakers to improve programs and services for all Californians.
Our office evaluates complex problems and recommends actionable solutions to help government provide efficient and equitable access to services for all Californians.
Our work is independent, nonpartisan, and results directly from the facts and data we collect.
When decision-makers act on our recommendations, real change happens. Because of our work, children have improved access to preventive health care, more California students are protected at our institutions of higher learning, there’s increased accountability in the spending of public funds, and small businesses can count on more fair equitable protections for California’s growing cannabis industry.
How Our Work Begins
Our audits and investigations are launched from different sources.
The Legislature
Legislators concerned about a program or agency can request a performance/policy evaluation through the bipartisan Joint Legislative Audit Committee (JLAC). The California State Auditor’s Office is involved from the beginning of this process. We review a legislator’s request for an audit and are available to answer questions when the request is formally made to JLAC. You can find more information on the JLAC audit request process on their Frequently Asked Questions (https://legaudit.assembly.ca.gov/content/faq) website.
If JLAC approves the request, our audit work begins. In this phase of the process, we gather the facts and dive into the details. Once we have analyzed all the evidence, we issue a public report. Everything we do is confidential until we publish our final report.
After we publish our reports, the Legislature may hold hearings and pass legislation to address the weaknesses we identified.
Whistleblower Tips
The California Whistleblower Protection Act authorizes the California State Auditor to receive whistleblower tips from state employees and members of the public who wish to report improper state government activity. Our office works diligently to investigate whistleblower tips of fraud, waste, and abuse of taxpayer funds, and provide recommendations to agencies to remedy these issues. All investigations are completely confidential unless the California State Auditor issues a public report.
For more on this process visit our Whistleblower webpage (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/whistleblower/) and be sure to check out our Whistleblower Frequently Asked Questions (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/whistleblower/#frequently-asked-questions).
State Laws
The California Legislature may pass legislation requiring the California State Auditor’s Office to conduct audits of programs, agencies, and governments, either on a one-time basis or continually. Examples of this legisation:
Alternative Whistleblower System Regulations: 2 CCR § 61300-61320
Redistricting Regulations: 2 CCR § 60800-60863
State High Risk Program: 2 CCR § 61000-61024
Local Government High Risk Program: 2 CCR § 61100-61140
California Healthcare, Research, and Prevention Tobacco Tax Act of 2016: 2 CCR § 61200-61240 (https://govt.westlaw.com/calregs/Browse/Home/California/CaliforniaCodeofRegulations?guid=I0986F16512064ABB8427E91C01DA1EB6&originationContext=documenttoc&transitionType=Default&contextData=(sc.Default))
High-Risk Issues
As required by Government Code section 8546.5, our office operates the High-Risk program to improve the operation of state government. We identify, audit, and recommend improvements to state agencies and statewide issues at high risk for waste, fraud, abuse, or mismanagement, or for having major challenges associated with their economy, efficiency, or effectiveness. Some current issues include state management of COVID-19 federal funds, water infrastructure, and information security. See the California State Auditor’s latest 2025 High-Risk report (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/reports/2025-601/).
Areas of Expertise
Looking for a job with the California State Auditor?
Explore Careers (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/careers/)
Performance & Policy Evaluations
As part of performance/policy evaluations—also known as performance audits—we collect evidence and find the truth. We use that truth to craft recommendations so that those in power can best serve the people they represent. Performance/policy evaluations involve systematically comparing what should be happening to what is happening. Our analyses and recommendations are objective, independent, nonpartisan, and based on evidence. We ultimately determine whether government agencies are efficient, effective, fulfilling their missions, and complying with the law. Our office is also responsible for audits that are mandated by state law, such as our annual review of the state judicial system.
Investigations into Improper Governmental Activities
If state agencies or employees are acting improperly, our team investigates them and develops reports to hold them accountable. Under the California Whistleblower Protection Act, we determine whether allegations of improper governmental activities are true and follow up to make sure they implement our recommendations for corrective action. We conduct investigations in response to complaints received from state employees, members of the public, or on our own initiative. We receive complaints by telephone, mail, fax, and through this website. Complainants have a right to remain confidential. More information can be found on our Whistleblower Hotline webpage (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/whistleblower/)
Financial & Compliance Audits
With billions of dollars in federal funding on the line, determining whether California’s financial statements are presented fairly is critical work. Each year, our staff conducts our annual audit of the State’s financial statements to ensure that California can receive funding that supports infrastructure, schools, and other public services. This audit—known as the Single Audit (https://information.auditor.ca.gov/stimulus)—is among the largest in the world and encompasses our evaluation of California’s financial statements, financial reporting safeguards, and compliance with laws, rules, and requirements. It satisfies the federal requirements for an independent financial audit and reviews the State’s compliance with federal program requirements.
Data Analytics
Our data analysts delve into large datasets to provide easily understood and visualized analyses to auditors, the Legislature, and the public. Our office can quickly clean and synthesize data to point in the right direction to address problems facing Californians.
State High-Risk Program
We investigate statewide issues and improve the operation of state government by identifying, auditing, and recommending improvements. We target state programs at high risk for waste, fraud, abuse, or mismanagement. We also audit programs experiencing major challenges associated with their economy, efficiency, or effectiveness.
Our Mission, Authority, & Standards
1
Our Mission
Our mission is to provide objective evaluations and effective solutions that enhance the transparency, accountability, and performance of California government for the people it serves. We follow the highest standards to provide stakeholders with reliable answers to problems in California government. We gather evidence to understand what an agency or program is meant to achieve, to determine whether it is falling short, and articulate what performance means for the people it serves.
2
Our Authority
State laws mandate our office be independent of the executive branch and legislative control. The California State Auditor is the only entity that has, by statute, full access to all records, accounts, correspondence, property, and other files of any publicly created entity, including state agencies, cities, counties, school districts, and special districts.
3
Our Standards
The California State Auditor’s Office conducts all performance and policy evaluations—also known as performance audits—in accordance with audit standards issued by the U.S. Comptroller General’s Government Accountability Office (GAO), including standards that we must follow as an independent auditor. To preserve the independence of our office and to ensure the receipt of federal funds, state law requires the State Auditor to follow those standards that explicitly free the auditor from control by the executive branch.
Awards & Recognition
2023
NSAA Excellence in Accountability Award
The National State Auditors Association (NSAA) selected the California Hospice Licensure and Oversight: The State’s Weak Oversight of Hospice Agencies Has Created Opportunities for Large-Scale Fraud and Abuse audit for the 2023 NSAA “Excellence in Accountability Award (https://www.nasact.org/accountability_awards).” Each year the NSAA recognizes the best performance audit (nationally) in various categories, including performance audits.The award was presented to representatives from our office at the 2023 NSAA Annual Conference in June.
2022
NSAA Excellence in Accountability Award
The National State Auditors Association (NSAA) selected Employment Development Department: Significant Weaknesses in EDD’s Approach to Fraud Prevention Have Led to Billions of Dollars in Improper Benefit Payments (Report #2020-628.2 (https://information.auditor.ca.gov/reports/2020-628.2/index.html), January 28, 2021) as the 2022 NSAA Excellence in Accountability Award (https://www.nasact.org/accountability_awards) for a small performance audit. Each year the NSAA recognizes the best performance audit (nationally) in various categories, including performance audits. The award was presented to representatives from our office at the 2022 NSAA Annual Conference in June.
2021
Gold Stevie Award for Government/Non-Profit Organization of the Year
In August 2021, the International Business Awards recognized the California State Auditor with a Gold Stevie Award as the best medium-sized government/non-profit organization of the year. The 2021 International Business Awards received over 3,700 entries from organizations in 63 nations and territories. Stevie Award winners were determined by the average scores of more than 260 executives worldwide who participated in the judging process from June through early August. The judges stated, “The California State Auditor has continued a high level of ongoing, focused growth.”
Certificate of Impact
Each year the National Legislative Program Evaluation Society (NLPES) recognizes reports, issued during the previous two years, in the field of legislative program evaluation that led to program improvements, dollar savings, and positive changes on public policy. The audits listed below were recognized by NLPES as having demonstrated significant impacts on state operations.

The Legislature
Legislators concerned about a program or agency can request a performance/policy evaluation through the bipartisan Joint Legislative Audit Committee (JLAC).
The California State Auditor’s Office is involved from the beginning of this process.
We review a legislator’s request for an audit and are available to answer questions when the request is formally made to JLAC.

If JLAC approves the request, our audit work begins.
In this phase of the process, we gather the facts and dive into the details.
Once we have analyzed all the evidence, we issue a public report.
Everything we do is confidential until we publish our final report.
After we publish our reports, the Legislature may hold hearings and pass legislation to address the weaknesses we identified.

2026 Peer Review results
Nonpartisan analyses for California’s policymakers to improve programs and services for all Californians.
Our office evaluates complex problems and recommends actionable solutions to help government provide efficient and equitable access to services for all Californians.
Our work is independent, nonpartisan, and results directly from the facts and data we collect.
When decision-makers act on our recommendations, real change happens. Because of our work, children have improved access to preventive health care, more California students are protected at our institutions of higher learning, there’s increased accountability in the spending of public funds, and small businesses can count on more fair equitable protections for California’s growing cannabis industry.
How Our Work Begins
Our audits and investigations are launched from different sources.
The Legislature
Legislators concerned about a program or agency can request a performance/policy evaluation through the bipartisan Joint Legislative Audit Committee (JLAC). The California State Auditor’s Office is involved from the beginning of this process. We review a legislator’s request for an audit and are available to answer questions when the request is formally made to JLAC. You can find more information on the JLAC audit request process on their Frequently Asked Questions (https://legaudit.assembly.ca.gov/content/faq) website.
If JLAC approves the request, our audit work begins. In this phase of the process, we gather the facts and dive into the details. Once we have analyzed all the evidence, we issue a public report. Everything we do is confidential until we publish our final report.
After we publish our reports, the Legislature may hold hearings and pass legislation to address the weaknesses we identified.
Whistleblower Tips
The California Whistleblower Protection Act authorizes the California State Auditor to receive whistleblower tips from state employees and members of the public who wish to report improper state government activity. Our office works diligently to investigate whistleblower tips of fraud, waste, and abuse of taxpayer funds, and provide recommendations to agencies to remedy these issues. All investigations are completely confidential unless the California State Auditor issues a public report.
For more on this process visit our Whistleblower webpage (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/whistleblower/) and be sure to check out our Whistleblower Frequently Asked Questions (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/whistleblower/#frequently-asked-questions).
State Laws
The California Legislature may pass legislation requiring the California State Auditor’s Office to conduct audits of programs, agencies, and governments, either on a one-time basis or continually. Examples of this legisation:
Alternative Whistleblower System Regulations: 2 CCR § 61300-61320
Redistricting Regulations: 2 CCR § 60800-60863
State High Risk Program: 2 CCR § 61000-61024
Local Government High Risk Program: 2 CCR § 61100-61140
California Healthcare, Research, and Prevention Tobacco Tax Act of 2016: 2 CCR § 61200-61240 (https://govt.westlaw.com/calregs/Browse/Home/California/CaliforniaCodeofRegulations?guid=I0986F16512064ABB8427E91C01DA1EB6&originationContext=documenttoc&transitionType=Default&contextData=(sc.Default))
High-Risk Issues
As required by Government Code section 8546.5, our office operates the High-Risk program to improve the operation of state government. We identify, audit, and recommend improvements to state agencies and statewide issues at high risk for waste, fraud, abuse, or mismanagement, or for having major challenges associated with their economy, efficiency, or effectiveness. Some current issues include state management of COVID-19 federal funds, water infrastructure, and information security. See the California State Auditor’s latest 2025 High-Risk report (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/reports/2025-601/).
Areas of Expertise

Performance & Policy Evaluations
As part of performance/policy evaluations—also known as performance audits—we collect evidence and find the truth. We use that truth to craft recommendations so that those in power can best serve the people they represent. Performance/policy evaluations involve systematically comparing what should be happening to what is happening. Our analyses and recommendations are objective, independent, nonpartisan, and based on evidence. We ultimately determine whether government agencies are efficient, effective, fulfilling their missions, and complying with the law. Our office is also responsible for audits that are mandated by state law, such as our annual review of the state judicial system.
Investigations into Improper Governmental Activities
If state agencies or employees are acting improperly, our team investigates them and develops reports to hold them accountable. Under the California Whistleblower Protection Act, we determine whether allegations of improper governmental activities are true and follow up to make sure they implement our recommendations for corrective action. We conduct investigations in response to complaints received from state employees, members of the public, or on our own initiative. We receive complaints by telephone, mail, fax, and through this website. Complainants have a right to remain confidential. More information can be found on our Whistleblower Hotline webpage (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/whistleblower/)
Financial & Compliance Audits
With billions of dollars in federal funding on the line, determining whether California’s financial statements are presented fairly is critical work. Each year, our staff conducts our annual audit of the State’s financial statements to ensure that California can receive funding that supports infrastructure, schools, and other public services. This audit—known as the Single Audit (https://information.auditor.ca.gov/stimulus)—is among the largest in the world and encompasses our evaluation of California’s financial statements, financial reporting safeguards, and compliance with laws, rules, and requirements. It satisfies the federal requirements for an independent financial audit and reviews the State’s compliance with federal program requirements.
Data Analytics
Our data analysts delve into large datasets to provide easily understood and visualized analyses to auditors, the Legislature, and the public. Our office can quickly clean and synthesize data to point in the right direction to address problems facing Californians.
State High-Risk Program
We investigate statewide issues and improve the operation of state government by identifying, auditing, and recommending improvements. We target state programs at high risk for waste, fraud, abuse, or mismanagement. We also audit programs experiencing major challenges associated with their economy, efficiency, or effectiveness.
Our Mission, Authority, & Standards
1
Our Mission
Our mission is to provide objective evaluations and effective solutions that enhance the transparency, accountability, and performance of California government for the people it serves. We follow the highest standards to provide stakeholders with reliable answers to problems in California government. We gather evidence to understand what an agency or program is meant to achieve, to determine whether it is falling short, and articulate what performance means for the people it serves.
2
Our Authority
State laws mandate our office be independent of the executive branch and legislative control. The California State Auditor is the only entity that has, by statute, full access to all records, accounts, correspondence, property, and other files of any publicly created entity, including state agencies, cities, counties, school districts, and special districts.
3
Our Standards
The California State Auditor’s Office conducts all performance and policy evaluations—also known as performance audits—in accordance with audit standards issued by the U.S. Comptroller General’s Government Accountability Office (GAO), including standards that we must follow as an independent auditor. To preserve the independence of our office and to ensure the receipt of federal funds, state law requires the State Auditor to follow those standards that explicitly free the auditor from control by the executive branch.

Our data analysts delve into large datasets to provide easily understood and visualized analyses to auditors, the Legislature, and the public. Our office can quickly clean and synthesize data to point in the right direction to address problems facing Californians.
State High-Risk Program
We investigate statewide issues and improve the operation of state government by identifying, auditing, and recommending improvements. We target state programs at high risk for waste, fraud, abuse, or mismanagement. We also audit programs experiencing major challenges associated with their economy, efficiency, or effectiveness.
Our Mission, Authority, & Standards
1
Our Mission
Our mission is to provide objective evaluations and effective solutions that enhance the transparency, accountability, and performance of California government for the people it serves. We follow the highest standards to provide stakeholders with reliable answers to problems in California government. We gather evidence to understand what an agency or program is meant to achieve, to determine whether it is falling short, and articulate what performance means for the people it serves.
2
Our Authority
State laws mandate our office be independent of the executive branch and legislative control. The California State Auditor is the only entity that has, by statute, full access to all records, accounts, correspondence, property, and other files of any publicly created entity, including state agencies, cities, counties, school districts, and special districts.
3
Our Standards
The California State Auditor’s Office conducts all performance and policy evaluations—also known as performance audits—in accordance with audit standards issued by the U.S. Comptroller General’s Government Accountability Office (GAO), including standards that we must follow as an independent auditor. To preserve the independence of our office and to ensure the receipt of federal funds, state law requires the State Auditor to follow those standards that explicitly free the auditor from control by the executive branch.
Awards & Recognition
2023
NSAA Excellence in Accountability Award
The National State Auditors Association (NSAA) selected the California Hospice Licensure and Oversight: The State’s Weak Oversight of Hospice Agencies Has Created Opportunities for Large-Scale Fraud and Abuse audit for the 2023 NSAA “Excellence in Accountability Award (https://www.nasact.org/accountability_awards).” Each year the NSAA recognizes the best performance audit (nationally) in various categories, including performance audits.The award was presented to representatives from our office at the 2023 NSAA Annual Conference in June.

Each year the NSAA recognizes the best performance audit (nationally) in various categories, including performance audits. The award was presented to representatives from our office at the 2022 NSAA Annual Conference in June.
2021
Gold Stevie Award for Government/Non-Profit Organization of the Year
In August 2021, the International Business Awards recognized the California State Auditor with a Gold Stevie Award as the best medium-sized government/non-profit organization of the year. The 2021 International Business Awards received over 3,700 entries from organizations in 63 nations and territories. **Evaluating audit requirements**

I'm considering the argument around the 10% requirement in audits. It's described as a recommendation rather than a mandate, which is an important nuance. The campaign states there’s "no mandate," but it still requires auditor recommendations for savings. Critics might exaggerate the implications, saying it forces cuts, but in reality, it encourages suggestions. Even though they're just recommendations, they can influence the analysis. Also, auditing special-tax programs could provide independent evidence for voters but only for specific instances.**Analyzing special tax proposals**

I'm examining the focus on special taxes and how voters might want to understand their uses. The fiscal cap limit is a significant policy, and it’s not just about spending limits on special taxes; it applies the Gann cap to all revenue. Leaders can spend within limits but can add new taxes as long as they comply. This doesn't restrict new taxes but makes them subject to the Gann cap, which closes potential loopholes and allows excess funds for schools or rebates when the cap is exceeded.**Understanding state appropriation limits**

I'm looking at how the Constitution allows the Legislature to change the state appropriation limit through a law, specifically Section 4 of Article XIII B, which lets them raise this limit with a 2/3 vote for capital outlays. I need to clarify how Prop 41 defines exclusions—it mentions revenue outside the General Fund and certain appropriations that don't count against this limit. It also prohibits any state tax from increasing the spending cap through statute, creating a significant restriction on the Legislature's power.**Evaluating Prop41 language**

I need to check the text of Prop41, especially concerning the 10% process. The auditors are independent, and their reports don't have to mandate a 10% cut with evidence. They can suggest budgetary savings without judging if funding needs to be less. However, the phrase "at least 10 percent" could lead to issues if they can't find savings, potentially forcing arbitrary recommendations. Also, comparing private-sector programs might not offer a direct comparison to public programs like healthcare.**Assessing audit concerns**

I'm noticing some significant concerns about the audits. First, they need to identify how program costs stack up against similar programs in the non-government sector, but if none exist, that could be a problem. The pre-election audit summary will be included in a voter guide, which could be costly. It seems like the audit only happens once 25% of signatures are collected for a new tax measure, which complicates things. Perhaps this is more of an analysis rather than a performance audit since no funds have been allocated yet.**Analyzing campaign funding**

The user is asking about support for a proposition, and I’m looking at recent election-day articles from November 3. I need to check campaign funding, which shows $58.3 million backing from a billionaire PAC against union-backed opposition. It’s interesting to note the majority comes from Building a Better California, driven by tech billionaires like Sergey Brin. This indicates significant financial interest in the outcome. I can verify how the campaign's funds relate to previous propositions, especially opposition finance.**Exploring funding sources and implications**

I’m considering if the "top donor" group also funds support for Prop 42 and opposition to Prop 40, which has been confirmed. It looks like there isn't an external campaign pushing against this. The SEIU and similar organizations benefit from federal healthcare funding and support Prop 40, showing their significant interests in healthcare. Billionaires are also involved, contributing resources. There’s a historical aspect with Prop 10 concerning spending exemptions. Furthermore, Prop 41 may restrict future initiatives approved by the majority unless amendments are made.**Evaluating tax ballot measures**

The conflict provision in 41 introduces a higher voting requirement for future ballot measures that aim to exempt a tax from limitations. If a new tax measure receives more votes, it can override 41, but if it doesn't, it becomes void. This adds a significant hurdle for future proposed special taxes. Voters might pass a tax measure but not support the necessary spending limit exemption, potentially creating confusion around competing measures and their requirements for approval.**Analyzing future tax measures**

Not all future tax measures need to be co-balloted with Prop41. As long as Prop41 remains law and isn't repealed, passing a tax exempt from the cap is impossible. If a later measure amends Article XXIV and gets more yes votes than 41, it can override it. However, the same-ballot conflict clause only applies to measures on the same ballot as Prop41, meaning a later measure can potentially amend or repeal the earlier one in subsequent elections.**Understanding ballot measures**

The rules about co-balloting mean that a later election can amend previous measures without permanently needing to outvote Prop41 when another tax comes up. Still, the operational prohibition on tax exemptions from Article XXIV means that a new tax initiative must explicitly alter Prop41 to be valid. It’s not a steep challenge, as voters still have the power. The Prop41 conflict measure only applies if another measure is on the same ballot, while Prop40 has its own conflict section to prevent being defeated by 41 or 42.

The conflict provision in 41 introduces a higher voting requirement for future ballot measures that aim to exempt a tax from limitations. If a new tax measure receives more votes, it can override 41, but if it doesn't, it becomes void. This adds a significant hurdle for future proposed special taxes. Voters might pass a tax measure but not support the necessary spending limit exemption, potentially creating confusion around competing measures and their requirements for approval.**Analyzing future tax measures**

Not all future tax measures need to be co-balloted with Prop41. As long as Prop41 remains law and isn't repealed, passing a tax exempt from the cap is impossible. If a later measure amends Article XXIV and gets more yes votes than 41, it can override it. However, the same-ballot conflict clause only applies to measures on the same ballot as Prop41, meaning a later measure can potentially amend or repeal the earlier one in subsequent elections.**Understanding ballot measures**

The rules about co-balloting mean that a later election can amend previous measures without permanently needing to outvote Prop41 when another tax comes up. Still, the operational prohibition on tax exemptions from Article XXIV means that a new tax initiative must explicitly alter Prop41 to be valid. It’s not a steep challenge, as voters still have the power. # About Us
## How Our Work Begins
The Legislature
Legislators concerned about a program or agency can request a performance/policy evaluation through the bipartisan Joint Legislative Audit Committee (JLAC).
The California State Auditor’s Office is involved from the beginning of this process.
We review a legislator’s request for an audit and are available to answer questions when the request is formally made to JLAC.
You can find more information on the JLAC audit request process on their Frequently Asked Questions website.
If JLAC approves the request, our audit work begins.
In this phase of the process, we gather the facts and dive into the details.
Once we have analyzed all the evidence, we issue a public report.
Everything we do is confidential until we publish our final report.
After we publish our reports, the Legislature may hold hearings and pass legislation to address the weaknesses we identified.
...
State Laws
The California Legislature may pass legislation requiring the California State Auditor’s Office to conduct audits of programs, agencies, and governments, either on a one-time basis or continually.
Examples of this legisation:
1. Alternative Whistleblower System Regulations: 2 CCR § 61300-61320
2. Redistricting Regulations: 2 CCR § 60800-60863
3. State High Risk Program: 2 CCR § 61000-61024
4. Local Government High Risk Program: 2 CCR § 61100-61140
California Healthcare, Research, and Prevention Tobacco Tax Act of 2016: 2 CCR § 61200-61240

# Report 2025-601 State High Risk Audit Program, Audit Plan: January 2026 through December 2027
In accordance with the state high-risk government agency audit program regulations, we present a tentative two-year plan for performing audits and conducting other monitoring activities.
The plan covers work from January 2026 through December 2027 regarding state agencies and statewide issues appearing on this state high risk list.
The plan is tentative, as such audits and monitoring are subject to resource availability based on our office’s projected workload.

State law authorizes my office to establish a high-risk government agency audit program for the purpose of identifying, auditing, and issuing reports on state issues that have major challenges associated with their economy, efficiency, or effectiveness.
Since 2013, the State’s deteriorating water infrastructure has been a recurring item on our state high-risk list.
Accordingly, my office conducted an audit of the oversight of dams and levees by the Department of Water Resources (Water Resources), Governor’s Office of Emergency Services (Cal OES), and the Central Valley Flood Protection Board.
Overall, we found that poorly maintained dams and levees continue to pose a risk to public safety.
...
In December 2025, the State Auditor’s Office issued its biennial assessment of statewide issues that represent a high risk to the State or its residents.
Conducted as part of our state high‑risk government agency audit program, that assessment concluded that the condition of the State’s dams and levees remains a high-risk issue.
...
The purpose of our state high-risk government agency audit program is to strengthen the operation of state government by recommending improvements for statewide issues that pose the potential to cause detriment to the State’s residents.
Consequently, we performed this audit to offer potential solutions to the issues the State is facing in overseeing its dams and levees.

About the California State Auditor
